title: William Floyd Estate
summary: In exchange for reconfirming previous land deeds between the Unkechaug and colonist Colonel William Tangier Smith, Smith granted in perpetuity one hundred and seventy-five acres of land to the tribe on Mastic Neck. The grant stated that the Unkechaug, " their children and the posterity of their children forever shall without molestation from me or my heirs or assigns shall and may plant and sowe forever " and added that the Indians could not sell, convey, or alienate this planting right or any part thereof to any.
activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: A historic 1700 agreement involving the lands surrounding the William Floyd Estate promised the Unkechaug people 175 acres in perpetuity, legally guaranteeing their right to plant and sow "without molestation" forever. The subsequent blurring of these deed boundaries and the loss of much of this promised acreage starkly illustrates how colonial legal systems consistently failed to uphold their own binding treaties with Native nations.
introduction_content:
The Floyd house and estate

The William Floyd House, also called the Nicholl Floyd House or Old Mastic House, was built by the Floyd family and remained connected to the family from the eighteenth century into the nineteenth. The estate's history is presented here alongside the continuing Unkechaug presence and land relationships around Mastic and Moriches.
preservation_content: The public estate provides the broad geographic context. Wigwam, planting, burial, and unverified archaeological locations are not identified.
